design_detail: Post-marketing surveillance case series from the independent steering committee (ISC) that the US FDA's Drug Abuse Advisory Committee recommended and the manufacturer, Ortho-McNeil, set up when tramadol (Ultram) was launched in the USA in April 1995 without scheduling. Reports came from spontaneous adverse-event reports to the company and to the FDA (MedWatch: patients, pharmacists, physicians) and from a paid network of key informants (110 NIDA-funded researchers and 145 other addiction experts, with access to about 250,000 people at risk for drug misuse). A subcommittee classified each of 1248 adverse-event reports received from 5 April 1995 to 31 March 2000 with DSM-IV-based ratings; withdrawal was rated only when there was no drug-seeking, and for this paper every withdrawal case was rescored as typical or atypical. Rates per 100,000 patients exposed used an exposure estimate built from tablets manufactured and sold and the average prescription size.
can_establish: That withdrawal after stopping tramadol, and in some reports after reducing or tapering it, was reported in at least 422 cases (546 counting reports rated as abuse) during its first five US years, which symptoms the reports described, and that about 1 in 8 rated withdrawal cases also had symptoms not typical of opioid withdrawal (severe anxiety and panic, confusion, derealization or paranoia, numbness or tingling, hallucinations).
cannot_establish: How often people who take tramadol have withdrawal when they stop (the rates are reported cases over estimated prescriptions, with unknown and, by the authors' own account, small capture); how long or how severe withdrawal is (no standardized measure; duration given only as an impression); who is at risk (age known in 139 cases, dose in 63–78%, no statistical comparison); or whether the atypical symptoms come from tramadol's effects on serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake (a hypothesis the authors leave open).

sample.recruitment: Other: spontaneous adverse-event reports (MedWatch, to the company and the FDA) and reports solicited quarterly from a key-informant network of 110 NIDA grantees and 145 other experts (clinicians, counsellors, methadone clinic directors), with access to about 250,000 people at risk; informants were offered $75 for each completed questionnaire and follow-up; the average response rate over the 20 quarters was 48.7% (p. 235, 2.2 Detailed methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Withdrawal ratings (Table 1, p. 235): 21, typical opioid-like withdrawal on stopping Ultram with no indication of abuse; 22, atypical opioid-like withdrawal with no indication of abuse. Any report with drug-seeking was rated as abuse or dependence (ratings 10–14, 20 and 30) even if withdrawal symptoms were present (p. 235). Typical withdrawal required at least three of the listed DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms (Table 2, footnote a, p. 236).
sample.demographics: Age known for 139 of 455 withdrawal cases (no figures given); sex known in 82% of typical and 87% of atypical cases, of whom about 56% were women (55.8% and 56.3%) (p. 237, 3.3). Length of exposure known in about 50% of cases and maintenance dose in 63% of typical and 78% of atypical cases (pp. 237–238, 3.4). No table of characteristics.
sample.attrition: Not applicable; large amounts of missing information instead (see demographics).
sample.selection_effects: Cases are those someone chose to report, either spontaneously or to a paid informant network aimed at people at risk for drug misuse; the authors cite an FDA estimate that spontaneous reports reflect only about 10% of adverse events and state that capture falls further over time (pp. 239–240). Reports with any drug-seeking were classified as abuse rather than withdrawal, which removes from the withdrawal count people whose withdrawal may have driven drug-seeking (124 abuse-rated reports had withdrawal symptoms, p. 237). Atypical symptoms were noticed as the study progressed and all cases were rescored afterwards (p. 235), so their recognition may have changed over time.

exposure.measurement: As stated by the reporter; prescription, amount and the stopping of tramadol were not verified. Length of exposure known in about half the cases and maintenance dose in 63% of typical and 78% of atypical cases (pp. 237–238).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Prescribed oral tramadol (Ultram). Reported maintenance amounts, as study conditions: typical cases 50–2000 mg per day, 92% at or below the 400 mg per day maximum recommended level; atypical cases 50–1300 mg per day, 25% above 400 mg per day. The exposures included many brief ones of 3–4 days, with no clustering in longer exposures (no counts given) (pp. 237–238, 3.4).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported. Other medicines and drugs taken by the people in the reports are not described; a history of drug misuse appears only in the Discussion (no difference between typical and atypical cases, p. 238) without data.

comparison.controls: None. Typical and atypical cases are compared descriptively (sex, dose); there is no comparison with people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal, or with people stopping another opioid.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Anxiety, panic, depressive or psychotic disorders before tramadol, concurrent antidepressants (relevant because the atypical symptoms resembled SSRI discontinuation) and other drug use are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Classification by an ISC subcommittee with the DSM-IV-based rating scheme in Table 1; typical withdrawal required at least three listed opioid withdrawal symptoms; atypical withdrawal was typical withdrawal plus a strong component of other CNS disturbances (p. 236). Atypical symptom groups are given as percentages of atypical cases (Table 2); rates per 100,000 patients exposed are plotted by quarter (Figure 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: No inter-rater reliability or validation of the typical/atypical split is reported; the authors say 'atypical' is a descriptor, not a claim that there are two syndromes (pp. 235–236).
outcomes.operationalization: A withdrawal case was a report rated 21 or 22: withdrawal on stopping (or reducing) tramadol with no drug-seeking and no other evidence of abuse.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical test is reported; the comparisons by sex, dose, age and exposure length are descriptive.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None described; raters classified the full content of each report.

analysis.effect_sizes: 422 withdrawal cases among 1248 adverse-event reports (Table 3: 33%; 33.8% by editors' arithmetic): typical 367 (86.97% of withdrawal cases, 29% of all reports), atypical 55 (13.03%, 4%). With the 124 abuse-rated reports that included withdrawal symptoms (121 typical, 3 atypical), at least 546 cases (43.8% of the 1248, editors' arithmetic). Among atypical cases: severe anxiety and panic 32.8%, unusual CNS symptoms 27.2%, unusual sensory phenomena 25.4%, hallucinations 20.0%. Rates: the text says total withdrawal reached 2.5–3.0 cases per 100,000 patients 12–15 months after launch and later fell below 1; Figure 1 peaks at about 2.3 in the quarter centred on May 1996 (37 typical and 10 atypical reports) and ends at about 0.3. Above 400 mg per day: 25% of atypical vs 8% of typical cases with dose data (counts not given). No confidence intervals.
analysis.selective_reporting: Age, exposure length and history of drug misuse are discussed without numbers; the counts behind the sex and dose percentages, and the estimated numbers of patients exposed behind the rates, are not given; the breakdown of the 644 abuse-rated reports and of the remaining reports is not given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over five years of US surveillance, 422 adverse-event reports were rated as withdrawal without drug-seeking (33% of all reports), 55 of them (13%) with symptoms beyond typical opioid withdrawal; the reporting rate peaked at about 2.5–3.0 cases per 100,000 patients 12–15 months after launch (the paper gives no time unit for it) and fell below 1 later; most typical cases with a known dose occurred at or below 400 mg per day; symptoms in mild cases were reported to settle within 2–3 days.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say withdrawal made up nearly 40% of all adverse events (pp. 233, 238), but Table 3 gives 33% (p. 237). The Discussion calls withdrawal the most prevalent adverse event (p. 238), while 644 reports were rated as abuse (p. 237). The rate is stated as 2.5–3.0 at its peak (p. 236), approximately 1 (p. 238) and less than 2 per 100,000 (p. 239), and the peak in Figure 1 is lower than the text; the authors call the rate "quite low" (p. 238) while arguing that spontaneous reports capture about 10% of events or less (pp. 239–240), so it is a floor, not an incidence. The suggestion that withdrawal may be more common in women (p. 237) has no exposure figures by sex. 'No difference in history of drug abuse' between typical and atypical cases (p. 238) is asserted without data. The conclusion that the withdrawal 'bears little relationship to abuse or dependence' (p. 239) follows from the rule that every case with drug-seeking was rated abuse. The management advice (gradual dose reduction; low-dose benzodiazepines for atypical symptoms, p. 238) rests on about 75 consultations, with no counts or outcomes.

timeline.event: Raffa et al.: opioid and non-opioid (noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake) components of tramadol's action, cited as the possible basis of the atypical symptoms (p. 238); not read

Cicero et al., the same committee's description of the surveillance programme and its abuse rates (1–1.5 cases per 100,000 patients) and of the exposure algorithm behind the rates (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 57, 7–22); not read
This report: 422 rated withdrawal cases, 55 of them atypical, April 1995 to March 2000

Rostam-Abadi et al., review of Iranian studies: two case reports of tramadol withdrawal (an adult with mental and physical symptoms after sudden cessation, titled 'Psychosis following tramadol withdrawal' in its reference list, and a neonate) and no study measuring withdrawal in people who stop tramadol

replication.where_it_stands: The only source in this set that describes atypical tramadol withdrawal in numbers; how often withdrawal, typical or atypical, follows stopping tramadol has not been measured in any study read here. Rostam-Abadi et al. (2020) cite laboratory studies of tramadol's physical dependence potential (for example Lanier et al., 2010), which were not read for this card.

funding.funder: A grant to Theodore J. Cicero from Ortho-McNeil Pharmaceuticals, Raritan, NJ (Acknowledgements, p. 240), the sponsor of Ultram (p. 234).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: The ISC was set up by the manufacturer on the FDA advisory committee's recommendation, and the company agreed that the ISC would notify the FDA and the company if Ultram needed to be scheduled (p. 234). One author's affiliation is a company (Gordon S. Black Corporation). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people taking tramadol for pain, or a randomized comparison of stopping abruptly against tapering, followed through discontinuation with a standardized opioid-withdrawal scale plus items for SSRI-type discontinuation symptoms, recording dose, duration, concurrent antidepressants and CYP2D6 status, with a comparison group stopping another opioid.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Reports reaching the company or the FDA plus a paid informant network focused on people at risk for misuse; not a frame of people prescribed tramadol.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: Cases enter only if someone reports them; reporting is voluntary or paid and its completeness is unknown.

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 422 cases are enough to describe the reported symptom patterns, but the number of cases depends on unknown capture, so size does not make the rates precise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age known for 139 of 455, sex for 82–87%, exposure length for about half and dose for 63–78%; no table of characteristics.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Under-reporting is not quantified; the informant response rate was 48.7%; reports with drug-seeking were moved to the abuse categories.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: DSM-IV criteria (at least three symptoms) for typical withdrawal applied by expert raters; the atypical category was created during the study without operational criteria, all cases were rescored afterwards, and no reliability data are given.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Information came from patients, pharmacists, physicians, the FDA and informants with varying completeness; no standardized assessment.

domains.domain: 8. Appropriate statistical analysis
domains.note: Rates without stated denominators or intervals, and sex and dose comparisons without counts or tests; the rate is stated three different ways.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Informant response averaged 48.7%, and the capture of spontaneous reports is unknown (the authors cite about 10%); neither is adjusted for.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI checklist has no overall algorithm; the editors summarize the risk of bias as high. The data are voluntary and paid reports of unknown completeness, classified by a committee funded through the manufacturer, with much missing information and no statistical analysis. The card may be cited for the existence and description of tramadol withdrawal, including symptoms atypical for opioids, in reports from the first five US years, and for the share of rated withdrawal cases that were atypical (55 of 422); not for how often people who stop tramadol have withdrawal, not for the size of the rates, and not for risk factors.

key_findings.finding: Reports came from two sources: spontaneous reports received by the drug's sponsor, Ortho-McNeil, from patients, pharmacists, physicians and the FDA (MedWatch), and a key-informant network of 110 NIDA grantees and 145 other experts with access to about 250,000 people at risk for misuse, offered $75 per completed questionnaire; the average informant response rate over the 20 quarters was 48.7%.

Withdrawal was rated only when there was no drug-seeking; reports with both withdrawal and drug-seeking were rated as abuse (ratings 10–14, 20 and 30). Because unusual symptoms appeared as the study progressed, all withdrawal cases of 1995–2000 were rescored as typical or atypical; typical withdrawal required at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms.
key_findings.locator: 2.2 Detailed methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 1 (p. 235); Table 2, footnote a (p. 236)

key_findings.finding: From launch in April 1995 to March 2000, 1248 adverse-event reports were classified; 422 (33%) were rated withdrawal: 367 typical (86.97% of withdrawal cases; 29% of all reports) and 55 atypical (13.03%; 4%), about 1 in 8.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 422 of 1248 is 33.8%. The abstract (p. 233) and the Discussion (p. 238) say withdrawal was nearly 40% of all adverse events.

key_findings.finding: Atypical cases had severe anxiety and panic attacks (32.8%), unusual CNS symptoms such as confusion, delusions, depersonalization, derealization and paranoia (27.2%), unusual sensory phenomena such as numbness, tingling, paresthesia and tinnitus (25.4%) and tactile, visual or auditory hallucinations (20.0%). Typical cases had symptoms such as abdominal cramps, anxiety, bone pain, depression, diarrhoea, goose flesh, insomnia, tearing, nausea, restlessness, runny nose and sweating (frequencies not given).
key_findings.note: The four percentages cannot all come from 55 cases: the nearest counts (18, 15, 14, 11) give 32.7%, 27.3%, 25.5% and 20.0% (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Of the 644 reports rated as positive, possible or alleged abuse, 121 had typical and 3 atypical withdrawal symptoms, so at least 546 withdrawal cases were reported in all.

Total withdrawal is said to have reached 2.5–3.0 cases per 100,000 patients 12–15 months after launch and then fallen below 1 per 100,000. Figure 1 prints the quarterly numbers of reports (typical 2 to 37, atypical 0 to 10 per quarter) and rates; the highest quarter, centred on May 1996, had 37 typical and 10 atypical reports.
key_findings.note: Read at 300 dpi: the quarterly counts printed on Figure 1 add up to 367 typical and 55 atypical, as in Table 3; the plotted peak of total withdrawal is about 2.3 per 100,000, below the 2.5–3.0 stated in the text, and the last quarter is about 0.3.

key_findings.finding: Age was known for only 139 of 455 withdrawal cases (no figures given; the authors say the ages appear to indicate that age is not an important predisposing factor). Sex was known in 82% of typical and 87% of atypical cases; about 56% were women (55.8% and 56.3%).

Length of exposure was known in about 50% of withdrawal cases and was a weak factor: many cases followed relatively brief exposures of 3–4 days, with no clustering after long exposure (no counts). Maintenance dose was known in 63% of typical cases (range 50–2000 mg per day; 92% at or below 400 mg per day) and 78% of atypical cases (range 50–1300 mg per day); the paper gives 25% of all atypical cases as above 400 mg per day, about three times the 8% of typical cases, without saying whether the base is all atypical cases or those with a known dose. Atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage.
key_findings.note: No counts or tests are given for the 25% vs 8% comparison.

key_findings.finding: Many physicians stopped Ultram abruptly despite the label's warning, and withdrawal also followed some tapered stops. Most reported cases were mild, were monitored without treatment and usually resolved within 2–3 days; in more severe cases some physicians restarted tramadol and tapered it slowly, others stopped it and treated atypical symptoms with low-dose benzodiazepines, and most atypical symptoms were said to respond. This rests on about 75 consultations by ISC clinicians; no counts are given.

The Discussion gives the withdrawal rate as approximately 1 case per 100,000 patients exposed (p. 238) and as less than 2 cases per 100,000 (p. 239), against 1–1.5 abuse cases per 100,000 in the committee's earlier report; phase I–III trials in about 5000 people had not suggested abuse or withdrawal.
The authors cite an FDA estimate that spontaneous reports reflect only about 10% of the adverse events that occur, and state that after several years they probably reflect considerably less than 5%.

The authors note that the atypical symptoms were more like those of SSRI antidepressant withdrawal than of opioid withdrawal and may relate to tramadol's noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition, which remains to be determined; they warn that without awareness these symptoms may be misdiagnosed as psychosis or delirium.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract (p. 233) and Discussion (p. 238) say withdrawal made up nearly 40% of all adverse events; Table 3 gives 422 of 1248, printed as 33% (editors' arithmetic: 33.8%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'nearly 40%' matches neither count (33.8% of reports rated withdrawal; 43.8% if the 124 abuse-rated reports with withdrawal symptoms are added), so it is not simply an overstatement; a claim should use one of these with its basis stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The withdrawal rate is given as 2.5–3.0 per 100,000 at its peak (p. 236), approximately 1 per 100,000 (p. 238) and less than 2 per 100,000 (p. 239); Figure 1 plots a peak of about 2.3 (p. 237). No overall rate, no denominators and no time unit are stated (the Methods describe a monthly rate, the figure is by quarter).
reporting_issues.consequence: None of the rate statements can be checked or turned into a risk; any claim should cite the quarterly reporting rates as minimum figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Age data are said to exist for 139 of 455 cases of withdrawal (p. 237), but the paper reports 422 rated withdrawal cases, or 546 with the abuse-rated reports.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator 455 matches neither count; the base of the age statement is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Atypical withdrawal is described as always accompanied by typical symptoms (p. 236, text), as often combined with them (Table 2, footnote b, p. 236), and as occurring in addition to, or in place of, typical withdrawal (p. 238).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether atypical symptoms can occur without opioid-type withdrawal cannot be told from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 is headed 'Age, sex, history' but reports no history data; the Discussion nevertheless states there was no difference in history of drug abuse between typical and atypical cases (p. 238).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about history of drug misuse has no supporting data in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Withdrawal is called the most prevalent adverse event (p. 238), but 644 of the same 1248 reports were rated as positive, possible or alleged abuse (p. 237), more than the 422 withdrawal reports.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ranking of withdrawal among adverse events is not supported as stated; the breakdown of the abuse ratings is not given.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says both kinds of withdrawal may be more common in women, then that the data do not appear to establish any relation with sex (p. 237); no figures for the sex of people prescribed tramadol are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 56% of women among reported cases cannot be read as a higher risk in women.
